title: いってらっしゃい  (Have a Good Day)

segments.t: At the front door, young Daisuke sees his father off to work and asks him to come home early. Muranishi claims he has overtime tonight, until sharp-eyed Mayumi spots arcade coins spilling out of his pocket. Listen to this morning send-off.
いってらっしゃい、パパ。
早く帰ってね！
今日は残業だから遅いんだよ。
どうせゲームでもやってサボってるくせに。
そんなこと言うなよ、真由美。
ほら！また小銭だ。
いや、これは仕事の小銭だよ。
頑張って遊んできて。
本当に仕事だからな。
じゃあ、行ってくる。
いってらっしゃい！
はーい。
Every Japanese home uses a matched pair of doorway greetings every morning. Let's hear how they work alongside Mayumi's teasing.
いってらっしゃい、パパ。
'Have a good day, Papa.' Anyone staying at home calls out "itterasshai" to the person stepping out the door—literally a polite 'please go and come back'.
早く帰ってね！
'Come home early, okay!' "Hayaku" turns "hayai", early or fast, into 'early', and "kaette ne" softens "kaeru", to return home, into a warm request.
今日は残業だから遅いんだよ。
'I have overtime today, so I will be late.' Office workers use "zangyou", overtime work, almost daily. Following it with "dakara", therefore or because, leads into "osoi", late.
どうせゲームでもやってサボってるくせに。

'Even though you are probably just playing games and slacking off anyway.' "Douse" shrugs 'anyway, I bet', and "sabotteru" comes from French 'sabotage'—the everyday slang word for skipping class or work!
そんなこと言うなよ、真由美。
'Do not say things like that, Mayumi.' Putting rough "na" right after dictionary-form "iu", to say, creates a blunt 'do not say that', softened a touch by "yo".
ほら！
'Look!' Whenever you point at proof right in front of someone's eyes, "hora" says 'look!' or 'see, told you!'
いや、これは仕事の小銭だよ。
'No, these are coins for work.' "Kozeni" pairs "ko", small, with "zeni", money—pocket change or loose coins for payphones and arcade cabinets.
頑張って遊んできて。
'Have fun playing hard out there.' Mayumi mischievously glues "ganbatte", do your best, onto "asonde kite", go have fun playing—mocking his fake overtime.
じゃあ、行ってくる。
'Well then, I am heading out.' Here is the other half of the doorway pair: the person leaving always says "itte kuru" (or polite "itte kimasu"), literally 'I will go and come back'.
はーい。
'Okay!' Stretching "hai" into cheerful "haai" sounds warm and playful when answering a child. Now let's listen to the whole doorway scene again.
いってらっしゃい、パパ。
早く帰ってね！
今日は残業だから遅いんだよ。
どうせゲームでもやってサボってるくせに。
そんなこと言うなよ、真由美。
ほら！また小銭だ。
いや、これは仕事の小銭だよ。
頑張って遊んできて。
本当に仕事だからな。
じゃあ、行ってくる。
いってらっしゃい！
はーい。
Remember that matched doorway pair—"itte kuru" when you head out, and "itterasshai" from the people waving you off—plus "hayaku kaette ne" to ask someone home early. See you next time.
またね。
